content: Actions to address tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis and treatment may include re-evaluating the patient for TB, conducting additional molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic (mWRD) tests, culturing more samples, and assessing the possibility of laboratory or clerical errors. If anti-TB therapy was initiated based on clinical judgment, the patient’s response to treatment should be carefully evaluated. For cases where mWRD results indicate Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) detected, rifampicin (RIF) resistance detected, but phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) shows RIF susceptibility, the mWRD result should guide treatment decisions while awaiting further testing. This discrepancy may arise from false-susceptible phenotypic results, as strains with certain mutations often fail RIF-based first-line regimens. In settings with low multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) prevalence, rare silent mutations may cause false-resistant mWRD results. Follow-up actions may include DNA sequencing, confirmatory testing on other mWRD platforms, phenotypic DST using solid media, and evaluating laboratory or clerical errors. If mWRD results show MTBC detected, RIF resistance not detected, but phenotypic DST indicates RIF resistance, the treatment regimen should be adjusted based on the phenotypic DST results. False RIF-susceptible mWRD results are rare but have been observed in 1–5% of RIF-resistant TB cases tested with Xpert MTB/RIF in various settings. Most RIF resistance is due to mutations in the rpoB gene region sampled by Xpert tests, but resistance can also arise from mutations outside this region, leading to false-negative RIF resistance results. Surveillance to monitor the emergence of such clones over time should be considered. Follow-up actions may include DNA sequencing, repeating phenotypic DST, and evaluating laboratory or clerical errors. For Xpert Ultra results of MTBC detected trace with negative culture, interpretation must consider patient characteristics, specimen type, and prior TB treatment history. Negative cultures may result from factors such as prior TB treatment, transport or processing issues, contamination, inadequate testing volume, or laboratory errors. Studies have shown that many MTBC detected trace and culture-negative results occur in individuals who completed therapy within the past 4–5 years, likely due to non-viable or non-replicating bacilli. These results must be interpreted in the context of prior treatment, and follow-up actions may include assessing therapy response, re-evaluating prior or current anti-TB drug use, and repeating culture or mWRD testing. The lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) test is recommended to aid TB diagnosis among people living with HIV (PLHIV), particularly in high HIV burden settings or for individuals meeting testing criteria. LF-LAM results are typically available within 15 minutes and can guide treatment decisions while awaiting mWRD results. LF-LAM has sufficient sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing TB in PLHIV but is less effective in HIV-negative individuals. The test is particularly useful for critically ill PLHIV or those with advanced HIV disease (AHD) and low CD4 counts. Negative LF-LAM results do not rule out TB, and mWRD results should be evaluated when available. Additional investigations, such as chest X-rays or clinical assessments, may be necessary. For hospitalized PLHIV, systematic TB testing with mWRD is recommended if TB prevalence exceeds 10%. LF-LAM testing should be performed in parallel with mWRD testing for rapid diagnosis and treatment initiation. All patients with TB symptoms capable of producing sputum should submit a sample for mWRD testing. For extrapulmonary TB, Xpert MTB tests are recommended for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lymph node aspirates, and other relevant specimens. Blood samples may also be used for disseminated TB in HIV-positive individuals. In outpatient settings, LF-LAM testing is recommended for PLHIV with advanced disease or low CD4 counts, regardless of TB symptoms. Treatment decisions should be based on LF-LAM results while awaiting mWRD results. Negative results from both tests do not rule out TB, and further evaluations, such as chest X-rays or additional clinical assessments, should be conducted. Treatment for bacterial infections or Pneumocystis pneumonia may also be considered, with clinical response evaluated after 3–5 days.
